To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Knowledge self-efficacy, enjoyment in helping others, reciprocity and organizational reward positively impact knowledge contributors’ EKR usage; (2) generalized trust, pro-sharing norm, and identification moderate the effects of codification effort and reward on EKR use; and (3) knowledge contributors’ loss of knowledge power, loss of image and knowledge self-efficacity are not moderated by any of the contextual factors.
the impact of extrinsic benefits on knowledge contributors' EKR usage is contingent upon particular contextual factors whereas intrinsic benefits do not appear to be moderated by such factors.
knowledge self-efficiency and enjoyment in helping other significantly impact EKR use by knowledge contributors.

the factors influencing the willingness of knowledge workers to contribute to knowledge repositories.
understanding the determinants of the use of EKRs by knowledge contributors.
the issue of knowledge contribution, and the results of this work can help organizations improve their KM initiatives by enhancing the knowledge contribution behavior of their employees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

EKR systems can be used to effectively facilitate knowledge exchange in organizations if knowledge contributors perceive them to be easy to use, and are rewarded by their organizations for sharing knowledge.
the findings of the study provide a theoretical basis for the design and implementation of EKRs that can facilitate the sharing of knowledge through these systems by employees.
the model developed in this study provides the most comprehensive and detailed understanding of EKR usage by employees in the literature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

knowledge contributors are more willing to contribute knowledge to an EKR if they feel they have the ability to do so, if they enjoy doing so, and if the EKR offers them extrinsic benefits contingent on particular organizational conditions.
the EKR usage is influenced by both the individual characteristics and the contextual factors.
knowledge contributors are more likely to use EKRs if they perceive that they are capable of using the systems, enjoy helping others, and are motivated by extrinsic rewards.
The main takeaway from our work is that
organizations can enhance knowledge sharing through EKRs by focusing on the intrinsic benefits of knowledge sharing.
knowledge contributors should be provided with the necessary resources to enhance their knowledge self-efficacies and enjoyment in helping other employees.
the success of KM systems is dependent on the extent to which they provide intrinsic and extrinsic benefits to contributors.
